messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Overanalysing: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo is a 22-year-old Latino HVAC technician who presented for an initial assessment reporting significant distress following an incident at a worksite approximately fourteen months ago. He was working alongside a senior colleague on a commercial rooftop unit when, in the course of repositioning a heavy refrigerant compressor, his grip failed. The equipment shifted and struck his colleague, a man in his forties named Derek, with enough force to send him over the low parapet edge. Derek survived but sustained a severe spinal injury that left him partially paralysed. Mateo had been the one directing the lift. In the seconds before the equipment moved, there had been an unusual stillness on the roof — the ambient noise of the city seemed to drop away — and then the sound of the impact, and then nothing but that same terrible quiet before Derek began to scream.

In the weeks that followed, Mateo continued working because stopping felt worse than moving. He told himself he needed to understand exactly what had gone wrong, and so he would lie awake reconstructing the sequence of events in minute detail — the angle of his hands, the precise moment his grip shifted, whether he had said something that distracted Derek at the wrong instant. The analysis never resolved into clarity. It only circled back on itself, each pass producing a slightly different version of his own culpability. He had come to believe, with a conviction that felt immovable, that he had not done enough to stop what happened — that there had been a window, however narrow, in which a better version of himself would have acted differently and Derek would still be walking.

That belief began to reorganise his life quietly and then all at once. On rooftop jobs, when the ambient noise of traffic and ventilation systems would momentarily fall away, Mateo's body would respond before his mind caught up — heart hammering, hands going cold, a wave of nausea that he could not reason himself out of. He started requesting ground-level assignments and found reasons to avoid rooftop work entirely, which his supervisor eventually noticed and questioned. He told the supervisor it was an equipment preference. What he did not say was that the smell of hot roofing membrane — a smell present on that afternoon — could arrive without warning and place him back on that roof with a vividness that felt less like memory and more like dislocation. The memory, when it came, did not feel like his own. It had a quality of watching someone else's footage, a figure who wore his face but whose catastrophic failure he could observe from a remove that offered no comfort.

Outside of work, Mateo narrowed his world considerably. He felt genuinely safe in only two places: his mother's kitchen and his own bedroom. Anywhere else carried a low-grade vigilance that was exhausting to maintain. Silence, in particular, had become threatening in a way he struggled to articulate — the quiet before something terrible, he called it. He began avoiding social gatherings, family events, and eventually the anniversary of the accident entirely, spending that day in his room with the television on at volume, filling the silence with noise.

What frightened him most, beneath all of this, was the sense that his body could no longer be trusted. His hands — the hands that had failed — felt like instruments of potential harm rather than tools he commanded. He had stopped playing guitar, something he had done since adolescence, because holding the neck felt wrong in a way he could not explain. He looked at photographs of himself from before the accident and recognised the face but not the person. The young man who had been proud of learning a trade, who had wanted to become a foreman by thirty, felt entirely remote.

Mateo sought help after Derek's wife contacted him through a mutual colleague. She did not write anything accusatory. She simply said Derek was asking about him. Mateo could not bring himself to respond, and the inability to do so — the paralysis of it — was what finally brought him to the clinic. He arrived hoping, he said quietly, to become someone who could at least write that reply.
